modules.title: Introduction to Melodyne Interface and Workflow
modules.content:
## Why the Right Interface Matters  

Imagine you’re in the middle of a recording session. The vocalist has just delivered a flawless take, but a few notes sit just a half‑step flat, and one phrase drifts out of time. You open **Melodyne**, and within seconds you need to locate those problem spots, make precise pitch adjustments, and bounce the edited track back into your DAW without missing a beat. The speed and confidence with which you move through Melodyne’s panels can be the difference between a tight‑tight mix and a rushed, second‑guessing session. This chapter equips you with a mental map of the interface and the workflow shortcuts that turn a daunting window into a streamlined editing cockpit.

---

## The Core Layout of the Melodyne Window  

Melodyne’s UI is deliberately compact, yet every element has a purpose. Understanding where each lives will let you jump straight to the tool you need.

| Panel | Location | Primary Function |
|-------|----------|------------------|
| **Edit Grid** | Center‑stage, dominant visual area | Displays notes (or “blobs”) that represent pitch, timing, and amplitude. All editing occurs here. |
| **Tool Bar** | Top of the window, just below the menu bar | Houses the selection, pitch‑draw, amplitude, and other manipulation tools. |
| **Transport** | Bottom‑center, beneath the Edit Grid | Play, stop, loop, and tempo controls; also shows current position and timecode. |
| **Inspector** | Right‑hand side, collapsible panel | Context‑sensitive details: note parameters, DNA data, scale information, and more. |

> **Tip:** You can hide any of these panels via *View → Panels* to free up screen real estate. The most common custom layout for vocal work keeps the **Edit Grid** and **Inspector** visible, while the **Transport** is tucked away when not looping.

### The Edit Grid in Detail  

- **Horizontal Axis (Time):** Measured in bars, beats, or seconds, depending on your **Transport** settings.  
- **Vertical Axis (Pitch):** Displayed as a piano‑roll; each line corresponds to a semitone.  
- **Blobs:** Rounded shapes that encode a note’s pitch, timing, and amplitude. Their size reflects the note’s **loudness**; color (when enabled) can indicate **formant** or **DNA** data.  

When you hover over a blob, a tooltip shows the exact pitch (e.g., **C4 85 cents**) and the note’s start/end times. Double‑clicking a blob opens a **note editor** in the Inspector, where you can fine‑tune the parameters numerically.

### The Tool Bar Essentials  

| Tool | Icon | When to Use |
|------|------|-------------|
| **Select** | Arrow | Default mode for moving, cutting, or deleting blobs. |
| **Pitch‑Draw** | Pencil with vertical line | Sculpt pitch curves directly on the Edit Grid. |
| **Amplitude** | Waveform | Adjust volume of individual notes without affecting the rest of the track. |
| **Formant** | “F” symbol | Shift vowel characteristics after pitch changes. |
| **Quantize** | Grid | Snap notes to a chosen rhythmic grid (used in Rhythm mode). |
| **Loop** | Circular arrows | Enable looping of a specific region for focused editing. |

You can toggle tools with **keyboard shortcuts** (see the Navigation section) or by right‑clicking a blob to bring up a context menu with the same options.

### The Transport Controls  

- **Play / Stop (Spacebar):** Starts playback from the current cursor position. |
- **Loop (L):** Turns looping on/off for the highlighted region. |
- **Tempo (T):** Adjusts the tempo displayed in the grid; useful when working with a tempo‑flexible vocal track. |
- **Metronome (M):** Click to hear the click while editing—essential for aligning phrasing. |

### The Inspector – Your Detail Dashboard  

The Inspector shows **dynamic fields** that change based on the selected object:

- **Note Data:** Pitch (in cents), start/end times, duration, amplitude, formant shift. |
- **DNA (Direct Note Access) Data:** For polyphonic material, you’ll see individual partials, their frequencies, and amplitudes. |
- **Scale & Chord Information:** When you enable **Scale Detection**, the Inspector highlights the nearest scale degree. |
- **Advanced Settings:** Quantize strength, snap options, and custom key signatures.

You can resize the Inspector panel by dragging its left edge, or collapse it entirely with the **“–”** button.

---

## Four Editing Modes – When to Deploy Each  

Melodyne’s power stems from its **mode‑based workflow**. Switching modes changes how the Edit Grid interprets the audio, and each mode shines in different musical contexts.

### 1. Melodic Mode  

- **What it does:** Treats the source as a **single‑note monophonic line** (e.g., lead vocal, solo instrument). Each blob corresponds to an individual note.  
- **Ideal for:** Standard vocal leads, solo instruments, spoken word with clear pitch contours.  
- **Key workflow tip:** Activate **Scale Detection** (Inspector → Scale) to see real‑time suggestions for the nearest diatonic note.  

### 2. Polyphonic Mode  

- **What it does:** Decomposes the audio into **individual partials** (harmonics) and groups them into **notes**. This mode can handle chords, dense harmonies, and even piano voicings.  
- **Ideal for:** Backing vocal stacks, choir sections, or any material where multiple pitches occur simultaneously.  
- **Key workflow tip:** Use the **“Split”** command (right‑click → Split) to isolate a chord into its constituent notes for targeted pitch correction.  

### 3. Rhythm Mode  

- **What it does:** Focuses on **timing** rather than pitch. The grid displays note **onsets** as vertical markers; you can shift them left or right, quantize, or stretch them.  
- **Ideal for:** Tightening up vocal phrasing, aligning spoken word to a groove, or correcting rhythmic drift in rap verses.  
- **Key workflow tip:** Enable **‘Quantize Strength’** in the Inspector to control how aggressively notes snap to the grid—set it between 0 % (no snap) and 100 % (hard snap).  

### 4. DNA (Direct Note Access) Mode  

- **What it does:** Provides **sample‑level** access to each partial within polyphonic material, allowing micro‑level pitch and formant adjustments without affecting the rest of the sound.  
- **Ideal for:** Fine‑tuning complex vocal harmonies, correcting a single out‑of‑tune partial in a choir, or creatively reshaping timbre.  
- **Key workflow tip:** Combine **DNA** with **Formant** tools to preserve natural vowel quality after aggressive pitch moves.  

> **Scenario:** You have a three‑part backing vocal recorded as a single track. Switching to **Polyphonic** lets you isolate each part, then toggling to **DNA** allows you to correct a stray harmonic in the alto line without disturbing the soprano or tenor.  

---

## Navigation Shortcuts – Moving Through Melodyne at Light Speed  

Memorizing a handful of shortcuts dramatically reduces the time spent hunting for tools. Below is the **essential set** for vocal editing; most DAWs allow you to customize these further in **Preferences → Keyboard**.

| Action | Shortcut | Remarks |
|--------|----------|---------|
| **Play / Stop** | **Space** | Starts playback from the cursor; stops on second press. |
| **Select Tool** | **V** | Returns to the default arrow cursor. |
| **Pitch‑Draw Tool** | **P** | Immediate access for sculpting pitch curves. |
| **Amplitude Tool** | **A** | Adjust note volume directly on the grid. |
| **Formant Tool** | **F** | Useful after pitch correction to retain vocal character. |
| **Zoom In / Out (Horizontal)** | **Ctrl + Mouse Wheel** (Win) / **Cmd + Mouse Wheel** (Mac) | Focuses on timing details. |
| **Zoom In / Out (Vertical)** | **Shift + Mouse Wheel** | Highlights pitch details. |
| **Loop Region** | **L** | Toggles looping for the highlighted segment. |
| **Quantize Selected Notes** | **Q** | Applies the current quantize settings from the Inspector. |
| **Undo / Redo** | **Ctrl + Z / Ctrl + Shift + Z** (Win) / **Cmd + Z / Cmd + Shift + Z** (Mac) | Always keep a habit of undoing early mistakes. |
| **Toggle Inspector** | **I** | Shows or hides the Inspector panel. |
| **Switch Editing Mode** | **Ctrl + 1‑4** (Win) / **Cmd + 1‑4** (Mac) | 1 = Melodic, 2 = Polyphonic, 3 = Rhythm, 4 = DNA. |
| **Snap to Grid On/Off** | **S** | Enables precise positioning; disable for free‑form edits. |
| **Add Marker (for reference)** | **M** | Places a temporary marker on the grid; useful for navigating to problem spots. |

> **Pro tip:** Combine **Shift** with any navigation shortcut to **extend the selection** (e.g., **Shift + Space** plays from the current selection’s start point).

---

## Customizing Preferences for a Streamlined Workflow  

Melodyne’s **Preferences** dialog (found under *Edit → Preferences* or *Melodyne → Settings* on macOS) lets you tailor the environment to match your working style. Below are the most impactful settings for vocal editing.

### 1. Display Preferences  

- **Show Note Names:** Turn on to see letter names (C4, D#4) on each blob—great for quick visual reference.  
- **Color Coding:** Enable **Formant Color** to differentiate vowel shifts; useful when you have multiple vocal takes stacked.  
- **Grid Resolution:** Set the default grid to **1/16** for pop/rock vocals; switch to **1/32** for more intricate phrasing (e.g., jazz).  

### 2. Audio Settings  

- **Analysis Resolution:** Choose **Standard (44 kHz)** for most vocal work. For extremely low‑frequency material (e.g., male choir), bump to **High (96 kHz)** to capture subtle overtones.  
- **Latency Compensation:** If you’re editing *in‑place* (i.e., not bouncing to a new track), enable **Automatic Latency Compensation** to keep playback perfectly in sync with the DAW.  

### 3. Editing Preferences  

- **Snap Strength:** Set a default snap strength of **70 %**; you can override per edit via the Inspector.  
- **Auto‑Quantize:** Turn on **“Auto‑Quantize on Note Creation”** for Rhythm mode—new notes will automatically snap to the grid, reducing manual steps.  

### 4. Keyboard Shortcuts  

- **Custom Mapping:** If you prefer **Alt** over **Ctrl** for certain commands, adjust them here. The interface also supports **MIDI controllers**; mapping a pedal to **Loop** or **Play** can free up hands for hands‑on editing.  

### 5. File Management  

- **Auto‑Save Interval:** Set to **5 minutes** to protect against crashes.  
- **Default Save Location:** Point to your project’s **/MelodyneEdits** folder; this keeps all temporary files organized and makes batch exporting easier later on.  

> **Practice Exercise:** Open *Preferences → Display*, enable **Note Names** and **Formant Color**, then close the dialog. Notice how the Edit Grid now immediately conveys pitch information without needing the Inspector. This visual cue will speed up your first pass over any vocal track.

---

## Putting It All Together – A Quick Walkthrough  

Below is a concise, step‑by‑step workflow that demonstrates the concepts above. Assume you have imported a vocal take into Melodyne (import covered later).

1. **Identify the editing mode**  
   - Press **Ctrl + 1** to switch to **Melodic** (the vocal is monophonic).  

2. **Activate scale detection**  
   - In the **Inspector**, click **Scale → C Major**. The nearest scale degree for each note lights up in green.  

3. **Locate the problem area**  
   - Use **Space** to play, then press **M** to drop a marker at the first off‑pitch note.  

4. **Select the offending blob**  
   - Hit **V**, click the blob, and observe its pitch value in the Inspector (e.g., **Bb4 ‑ 30 cents**).  

5. **Correct the pitch**  
   - Switch to **Pitch‑Draw** (**P**), click and drag the blob upward until the cents read **0 cents** (or the nearest scale‑tonic).  

6. **Preserve vowel quality**  
   - With the blob still selected, hit **F** (Formant Tool) and lightly adjust the formant slider in the Inspector to keep the vocal sounding natural.  

7. **Check timing**  
   - Press **Ctrl + 3** to enter **Rhythm** mode, then verify the note aligns with the grid. Use **Q** (Quantize) if needed, adjusting the **Quantize Strength** to 80 % for a subtle lock‑in.  

8. **Loop the edited phrase**  
   - Drag a region around the corrected phrase, press **L** to loop, and listen repeatedly to ensure the edit sounds seamless.  

9. **Finalize**  
   - Save the project (**Ctrl + S**) and optionally export the corrected audio (**File → Export Audio**) for later DAW import.  

This micro‑workflow illustrates how the **Edit Grid**, **Inspector**, **Tool Bar**, and **Transport** interlock, and how switching modes and leveraging shortcuts can keep you in the creative flow.

---

## Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Remedy |
|---------|----------------|--------|
| **Accidentally editing the wrong mode** | Switching modes without checking the status bar. | Keep an eye on the **mode indicator** (top‑left of the window) or assign a dedicated shortcut to each mode. |
| **Over‑quantizing rhythmic feel** | Applying 100 % quantize to a vocal that should retain human groove. | Use the **Quantize Strength** slider; start at 50 % and audition. |
| **Formant drift after large pitch shifts** | Pitch‑draw moves the fundamental but leaves formants unchanged, causing a “chipmunk” effect. | After pitch correction, engage the **Formant Tool** and adjust until the vocal timbre feels natural. |
| **Cluttered workspace slowing navigation** | All panels visible can overwhelm the eye, especially on smaller monitors. | Collapse the **Transport** and **Inspector** when not needed; use **I** to toggle the Inspector quickly. |
| **Latency mismatch when editing in‑place** | Playback sounds ahead/behind the original DAW timeline. | Enable **Automatic Latency Compensation** in Preferences, or bounce the edited audio to a new track. |

---

## Extending the Workflow – Integration with Your DAW  

While this chapter focuses on the internal Melodyne environment, a smooth hand‑off to your DAW completes the loop. The most efficient method is to **run Melodyne as a plugin** inside your DAW’s track:

1. Insert **Melodyne** on the vocal track.  
2. Use the DAW’s **transport controls** (play, stop, loop) to sync with Melodyne, eliminating the need to switch windows.  
3. When finished, **render** the track **in place** (or bounce) to lock in the edits, preserving CPU resources.

Because the DAW’s **undo stack** typically includes Melodyne edits, you can revert an entire session of changes with a single DAW‑level **Undo** command—another powerful workflow safeguard.

---

## Recap of Core Concepts  

- The **Edit Grid** is the canvas; **Tool Bar** provides the brush; **Transport** controls playback; **Inspector** offers the microscope.  
- **Four editing modes** (Melodic, Polyphonic, Rhythm, DNA) each serve distinct musical situations.  
- Mastering **navigation shortcuts** and **custom preferences** turns Melodyne from a “tool” into an **extension of your musical intuition**.  

These fundamentals set the stage for deeper pitch‑correction techniques explored in later chapters.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Identify the four main panels** (Edit Grid, Tool Bar, Transport, Inspector) and know their primary roles.  
- **Choose the appropriate editing mode**: Melodic for single‑note vocals, Polyphonic for chords, Rhythm for timing, DNA for granular harmonic control.  
- **Leverage essential shortcuts** (Space, V, P, A, F, L, Q, I, and mode switches) to accelerate editing.  
- **Customize Preferences**—display options, audio analysis resolution, snap strength, and auto‑save—to match your workflow and reduce visual clutter.  
- **Apply a concise workflow**: select mode → locate problem → edit pitch/timing → adjust formant → loop for audition → save/export.  

By internalizing these interface fundamentals, you’ll spend less time searching for tools and more time shaping vocal performances that sit perfectly in the mix.

modules.title: Core Pitch Correction Concepts
modules.content:
## A Real‑World Call‑And‑Response

Imagine you’re mixing a pop vocal that just recorded a powerful chorus. The singer hits every lyric with emotion, but a few notes sit just a half‑step flat, and a couple of sustained vowels sound thin. You have two choices: **fix** the off‑pitch notes so the melody sits perfectly in the key, or **re‑imagine** the line by turning those same pitch quirks into a stylized, melodic hook. The decision hinges on understanding what “pitch” really is, how it interacts with a singer’s **intonation** and **formants**, and how Melodyne translates those acoustic details into editable data.

Below we unpack the musical and technical foundations that let you make that choice confidently, and we walk through how Melodyne detects pitch and visualizes it as the blobs you already saw on the Edit Grid.

---

## 1. Pitch, Intonation, and Formants in Vocal Performance  

### 1.1 What Is Pitch?  

* **Pitch** is the perceptual correlate of a sound’s fundamental frequency (F₀). In the human voice, F₀ is produced by the vibration of the vocal folds.  
* Musically, pitch is mapped onto a **musical scale** (e.g., C‑major) and quantified in **cents**—100 cents = one semitone.  
* On the Edit Grid, the **Vertical Axis (Pitch)** shows each blob’s nominal pitch (e.g., C4 85 cents).  

### 1.2 Intonation: The Human Factor  

* **Intonation** describes how accurately a singer’s produced pitches align with the intended musical pitch. Perfect intonation = 0 cents deviation.  
* Small deviations are normal and can be expressive (e.g., a slight rise on a phrase’s end). Large deviations (> 50 cents) often sound out‑of‑key.  
* Intonation is influenced by:  
  1. **Physiological factors** – tension of the vocal folds, breath support.  
  2. **Acoustic context** – interaction with accompaniment, room resonance.  
  3. **Artistic intent** – stylistic bends, vibrato, or genre‑specific pitch slides.  

### 1.3 Formants: The Voice’s Timbre Skeleton  

* **Formants** are resonant peaks in the vocal tract’s frequency response that shape vowel quality. The first two formants (F₁, F₂) determine the perceived vowel (e.g., “ah” vs. “ee”).  
* Formants are **independent of pitch**; you can raise the fundamental while the vowel sounds unchanged—think of a singer singing a high “ah” without sounding “ee”.  
* In Melodyne, the **Formant** attribute of a blob lets you adjust timbre without affecting pitch, preserving natural vowel shape when correcting intonation.  

> **Quick Reference**  
> - **Pitch** = fundamental frequency (F₀) → musical note.  
> - **Intonation** = pitch accuracy relative to target note.  
> - **Formants** = resonant frequencies shaping vowel quality, separate from pitch.  

---

## 2. Corrective vs. Creative Pitch Editing  

### 2.1 Corrective Editing: Restoring Musical Accuracy  

The primary goal is to bring the vocal **into tune** without altering its natural character. Typical situations:  

1. **Flat or sharp notes** that disrupt chord progressions.  
2. **Uneven vibrato** that sounds jittery.  
3. **Pitch drift** in sustained notes (e.g., “wow” moments).  

**Key principles**  

* **Preserve dynamics** – keep the original amplitude envelope; avoid flattening the performance.  
* **Maintain formants** – avoid “chipmunk” artifacts by leaving formant values untouched or using Melodyne’s formant‑preserving algorithms.  
* **Use quantization sparingly** – snap notes to the nearest scale degree only when the performance truly needs it; over‑quantizing creates robotic sounds.  

### 2.2 Creative Editing: Turning Pitch Into a Musical Tool  

When pitch becomes a **creative resource**, you can reshape the melody, generate harmonies, or sculpt unconventional textures. Common creative moves:  

1. **Pitch‑draw** a glide that wasn’t there, turning a static note into a swooping “slide”.  
2. **Re‑harmonize** a line by moving select notes to a different chord tone, creating surprise.  
3. **Formant morphing** – shift formants to produce an otherworldly vowel while keeping pitch intact.  

**Creative mindset**  

* **Intent first** – decide what emotional or sonic effect you want before moving any blob.  
* **Blend, don’t replace** – often a subtle pitch shift (e.g., +15 cents) can add tension without sounding out of key.  
* **Leverage Melodyne’s DNA** (though covered later) – fine‑tune micro‑details that give a natural feel to extreme edits.  

### 2.3 Decision Flowchart  

| Situation | Goal | Recommended Approach |
|-----------|------|-----------------------|
| Off‑key note in a tight pop mix | Preserve vocal character | Small pitch correction, keep formants, minimal quantization |
| Flat note that clashes with a chord | Tight harmonic alignment | Quantize to nearest scale degree, double‑check formants |
| Desire for a “glide” effect on a held vowel | Add expressive movement | Use Pitch‑Draw, optionally adjust formants for smoothness |
| Want a layered harmony that wasn’t recorded | Expand harmonic texture | Duplicate track, shift selected notes, preserve formants |

---

## 3. How Melodyne Detects Pitch  

### 3.1 The Underlying Algorithm (A High‑Level View)  

Melodyne’s pitch‑detection engine works in three stages:  

1. **Pre‑analysis** – the audio is split into short frames (≈ 10 ms). Each frame undergoes a **Fourier Transform** to extract frequency information.  
2. **Fundamental Estimation** – the algorithm identifies the strongest periodic component, assuming it corresponds to the vocal folds’ vibration.  
3. **Pitch Tracking** – consecutive frames are linked using a **dynamic programming** approach that favors smooth, musically plausible transitions.  

The result is a **continuous pitch curve** that Melodyne displays as a series of **blobs** on the Edit Grid.  

### 3.2 From Waveform to Blob  

| Step | What You See in Melodyne | What It Represents |
|------|--------------------------|--------------------|
| **Analysis** | Real‑time waveform scrolling while the **Transport** runs | Raw audio data |
| **Detection** | Blobs appearing on the Edit Grid, each with a vertical position (pitch) and horizontal width (duration) | Segments of stable pitch |
| **Attribute Assignment** | Inspector shows **loudness**, **formant**, **DNA** values for each blob | Acoustic characteristics of that segment |

* **Blob size** roughly reflects the stability of the pitch: a larger, more rectangular blob indicates a steady note; a narrow, irregular blob signals rapid pitch movement (e.g., a melisma).  
* **Cents offset** (e.g., C4 85 cents) is displayed when you hover or select a blob, letting you see the exact deviation from the nearest equal‑tempered pitch.  

### 3.3 Accuracy Limits  

* **Monophonic vs. Polyphonic** – In this chapter we assume **monophonic** material (single‑voice vocal). Polyphonic detection (multiple notes simultaneously) is covered later.  
* **Noise and Breath** – Heavy breath sounds or background noise can confuse the detector, producing **spurious blobs**. The Inspector’s **loudness** meter helps you spot and delete them.  
* **Formant‑heavy vowels** – Certain vowels (e.g., “oo”) have strong formant peaks that may be misidentified as pitch. Melodyne’s **formant‑preserve** mode mitigates this, but manual verification is still recommended.  

---

## 4. Reading the Edit Grid: Blobs as Editable Data  

### 4.1 Anatomy of a Blob  

When you click a blob, the **Inspector** reveals a set of parameters:  

* **Pitch** – displayed in note name and cents offset.  
* **Amplitude (Loudness)** – the perceived volume of that segment.  
* **Formant** – the vowel’s resonant characteristic, editable without affecting pitch.  
* **DNA** – a compact representation of the note’s spectral texture (used for fine‑tuning later).  

Understanding each field lets you decide **what** to edit and **how** to preserve the vocal’s naturalness.  

### 4.2 Editing Workflow Overview  

1. **Select** the target blob(s) using the **Select** tool.  
2. **Assess** pitch deviation (cents) in the Inspector.  
3. **Choose** an editing mode:  
   * **Pitch‑Draw** – manually redraw the pitch curve.  
   * **Quantize** – snap to nearest scale degree (use with caution).  
   * **Formant** – adjust vowel quality while leaving pitch untouched.  
4. **Listen** – toggle **Play / Stop** (Spacebar) to audition changes in real time.  
5. **Iterate** – use **Loop** (L) to focus on a short phrase if needed.  

### 4.3 Practical Example: Fixing a Flat Note  

*Scenario*: The vocalist sings an A4 that lands **‑45 cents** (almost a quarter‑tone flat) in the chorus.  

**Step‑by‑step**  

1. **Zoom** into the measure using the **Horizontal Axis (Time)** controls.  
2. **Click** the A4 blob; the Inspector now reads “A4 ‑45 cents”.  
3. **Activate** the **Pitch‑Draw** tool.  
4. **Drag** the blob upward until the cents read **0 cents** (or within ±5 cents for a natural feel).  
5. **Check** the **Formant** value – it should remain unchanged; if the vowel sounds thin after the pitch shift, nudge the Formant slider slightly upward to restore warmth.  
6. **Play** the corrected phrase, toggle **Loop** to repeat, and compare with the original.  

By preserving the original **Amplitude** and **Formant**, the corrected note retains its expressive dynamics while now sitting correctly in the key.  

### 4.4 Creative Twist: Adding a Glide  

*Scenario*: The same A4 is a perfect platform for a dramatic slide up to B4, turning a static note into a hook.  

**Steps**  

1. **Select** the A4 blob and the following B4 blob (hold **Shift** to multi‑select).  
2. Switch to **Pitch‑Draw**.  
3. **Draw** a smooth upward curve connecting the two blobs, ensuring the transition spans the desired duration (e.g., 500 ms).  
4. **Fine‑tune** the **Formant** of the intermediate region to avoid a sudden vowel change—drag the Formant slider gently upward if the glide sounds “nasal”.  
5. **Listen** in **Loop** mode, adjust the curve’s slope until the glide feels natural.  

The result is a **creative pitch edit** that adds melodic interest without sacrificing vocal realism.  

---

## 5. From Theory to Practice: Applying Core Concepts  

### 5.1 Quick Checklist Before Editing  

| ✔️ | Item |
|----|------|
| 1️⃣ | Confirm the track is **monophonic** (no overlapping notes). |
| 2️⃣ | Identify the **target scale** (e.g., C major) and note any **key changes**. |
| 3️⃣ | Scan the Edit Grid for **spurious blobs** (low loudness, erratic pitch). |
| 4️⃣ | Decide whether the edit is **corrective** (maintain original character) or **creative** (re‑imagine). |
| 5️⃣ | Note any **formant anomalies** that may need adjustment after pitch changes. |

### 5.2 Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Why It Happens | Remedy |
|---------|----------------|--------|
| **“Chipmunk” effect** | Pitch shifted without formant compensation | Keep the **Formant** value constant or use Melodyne’s **Formant‑preserve** mode. |
| **Over‑quantization** | Snap‑to‑grid on expressive vibrato | Use **Quantize** only on isolated off‑key notes, not on continuous vibrato. |
| **Abrupt vowel changes** | Large pitch moves crossing formant boundaries | Adjust **Formant** gradually while drawing pitch curves. |
| **Unwanted artifacts from breath** | Breath noise misidentified as a note | Delete low‑loudness blobs or isolate the vocal track pre‑analysis. |

---

## 6. Putting It All Together: A Mini‑Project  

**Goal**: Take a 12‑second vocal phrase, correct its intonation, and add a subtle creative glide at the end.  

1. **Import** the vocal into Melodyne (refer to the earlier “Preparing and Importing Vocal Tracks” chapter when you get there).  
2. **Analyze** – let Melodyne generate blobs on the Edit Grid.  
3. **Correct** – locate any blobs outside ±25 cents, use **Pitch‑Draw** to bring them within the ±5‑cents window. Preserve formants.  
4. **Create a Glide** – select the final note, draw a gentle upward curve of ~200 ms, adjust formants to smooth the transition.  
5. **Loop** the phrase, listen, and fine‑tune until the corrected and creative elements feel cohesive.  

Through this workflow you’ll have exercised **pitch detection**, **blob editing**, **intelligent formant handling**, and the **corrective vs. creative** decision process—all core concepts that underpin effective vocal pitch correction.  

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Pitch** is the fundamental frequency; **intonation** measures its accuracy; **formants** shape vowel quality independent of pitch.  
- **Corrective editing** restores pitch accuracy while preserving the vocal’s natural timbre; **creative editing** uses pitch as a compositional tool.  
- Melodyne detects pitch by analyzing short‑time Fourier data, linking frames into a continuous curve, and visualizing each stable segment as a **blob** on the Edit Grid.  
- The **Inspector** reveals each blob’s pitch (cents), amplitude, formant, and DNA—allowing precise, musically aware edits.  
- Effective pitch correction balances **musical intent** with **technical fidelity**: keep formants stable, avoid over‑quantization, and use the **Loop** and **Play** controls for iterative listening.  

By mastering these foundations, you’re ready to move into the next chapter—preparing and importing vocal tracks—where the practical workflow will build directly on the concepts explored here.

modules.title: Preparing and Importing Vocal Tracks
modules.content:
## A Vocal Take That Saves the Mix  
You’ve just captured a lead vocal in a live‑room session that sounds great—tight timing, emotive phrasing, and just the right amount of grit. The only thing standing between this performance and a polished production is the **pitch‑correction stage**. If the audio is imported into Melodyne with the wrong sample rate, an inappropriate detection mode, or without proper gain‑staging, even the most skilled editor will waste time fighting artifacts rather than shaping the performance. This chapter walks you through the exact workflow that prepares a vocal track for flawless pitch editing, so you can spend more time on musical decisions and less on technical clean‑ups.

---

## 1. Exporting the Vocal from Your DAW  

### 1.1 Choose the Right Resolution  
The resolution you select when bouncing the track determines how much headroom Melody Ne has for processing.

| Parameter | Recommended Setting for Vocals | Why It Matters |
|-----------|--------------------------------|----------------|
| **Sample Rate** | 44.1 kHz or 48 kHz (match your project) | Higher rates give more accurate timing detection but increase file size. Matching the DAW’s rate avoids resampling artifacts. |
| **Bit Depth** | 24 bit (or 32‑bit float if available) | Provides extra dynamic range for later gain adjustments and reduces quantisation noise during pitch manipulation. |

> **Tip:** If your session runs at 96 kHz, keep the export at 96 kHz. Down‑sampling later in Melodyne adds unnecessary conversion steps.

### 1.2 File Format Matters  
- **WAV** – Uncompressed, universally supported, preserves full resolution.  
- **AIFF** – Same benefits as WAV on macOS‑centric setups.  
- **FLAC** – Lossless compression; acceptable but some older plugins may not read it reliably.  

Avoid MP3 or other lossy formats; they introduce pre‑existing artifacts that become amplified during pitch correction.

### 1.3 Consolidate the Take  
If the vocal track contains multiple takes or comping edits, **render a single, continuous audio file** that includes the final comp. This ensures the Edit Grid in Melodyne reflects the exact timeline you intend to edit.

1. Solo the vocal bus.  
2. Disable any post‑effects (reverb, delay, compression) that you plan to re‑apply later.  
3. Bounce/render to the chosen format.  

---

## 2. Importing the Audio into Melodyne  

### 2.1 Opening the File  
1. Launch Melodyne (the version you’re using—Essential, Assistant, Editor, or Studio).  
2. From the **File** menu, choose **Open…** and navigate to the exported WAV/AIFF.  
3. Drag‑and‑drop is also supported; dropping the file onto the **Edit Grid** automatically creates a new instance.

### 2.2 Verify Project Settings  
Once the file appears in the **Edit Grid**, glance at the **Inspector** panel:

- **Sample Rate** – Should match the exported file. If it shows a different value, click the gear icon and select “Match Project Settings.”  
- **Bit Depth** – Displayed for reference; Melodyne works internally at 32‑bit float, but the original depth informs your gain‑staging decisions.

If any mismatch appears, re‑import the file after correcting the export settings in your DAW.

---

## 3. Selecting the Correct Detection Algorithm  

Melodyne offers two primary detection modes for vocal material:

| Mode | Ideal Use‑Case | How It Works |
|------|----------------|--------------|
| **Monophonic** | Solo vocals, single‑note lines, spoken word | Analyzes one pitch per time slice, delivering clean, precise blobs. |
| **Polyphonic** | Choirs, layered harmonies, background vocal stacks | Detects multiple simultaneous pitches; more processing‑intensive and may produce “ghost” notes. |

### 3.1 Determining the Right Mode  
1. **Listen to the track** – Is there any overlap of notes (e.g., double‑tracked choruses)?  
2. **Check the waveform** – Simultaneous peaks indicate polyphonic content.  
3. **Consider the editing goal** – If you only need to correct the lead line, **Monophonic** is usually sufficient, even for double‑tracked takes, because Melodyne will treat the combined signal as a single pitch contour.

### 3.2 Switching Modes in Melodyne  
- Click the **Detection Mode** dropdown in the **Inspector**.  
- Choose **Monophonic** for solo leads, **Polyphonic** for dense vocal arrangements.  
- After selection, press **Detect** (or the **Auto‑Detect** button) to let Melodyne analyse the audio.

> **Warning:** Running the Polyphonic algorithm on a purely monophonic track can create spurious blobs that clutter the Edit Grid, making subsequent pitch editing slower and less accurate.

---

## 4. Pre‑Processing: Gain Staging & Noise Reduction  

Before you dive into the Edit Grid, a clean, well‑leveled waveform makes the detection algorithm more reliable and reduces the risk of unwanted artifacts.

### 4.1 Gain Staging Inside Melodyne  

1. **Normalize the Track** – In the **Inspector**, click **Normalize** (or use the **Amplitude** tool). Set the target peak at **-6 dBFS**.  
   - This gives you headroom for later **Amplitude** edits without clipping.  
2. **Fine‑Tune the Overall Level** – Use the **Amplitude** slider to bring the vocal into the same RMS range as the rest of your mix (typically around **-18 dBFS** for a lead vocal).  
3. **Check for Clipping** – The **Peak** meter should stay well below 0 dBFS. If you see red clipping, lower the amplitude or re‑export a lower‑gain version from the DAW.

### 4.2 Noise Reduction Before Detection  

Even though Melodyne’s algorithms are robust, excessive background noise can confuse pitch detection, especially in quiet passages.

**Option A – Built‑in Noise Gate (if your DAW has one):**  
- Insert a gate before rendering the vocal file.  
- Set **Threshold** just above the noise floor; keep **Release** short to preserve natural decay.

**Option B – Dedicated Noise‑Reduction Plug‑in:**  
- Apply a **single‑band** or **spectral** noise reducer (e.g., iZotope RX, Waves X‑Noise) **only** on the exported file.  
- Aim for a **Noise Reduction** amount that removes hiss without making the vocal sound “processed.”  

**Tip:** After noise reduction, re‑export the cleaned file and re‑import into Melodyne. This extra step is worthwhile when the recording contains HVAC hum, distant crowd chatter, or mic bleed.

### 4.3 Quick Spectral Check  

Open the **Spectrogram** view in Melodyne (via the **View** menu). Scan for any stray frequencies that look like clicks, pops, or low‑frequency rumble. If you spot them:

- Use the **Amplitude** tool to lower the offending blobs.  
- For stubborn artifacts, consider a brief **Audio‑Edit** (cut or fade) within the DAW before re‑import.

---

## 5. Verifying the Imported Track Is Ready for Pitch Editing  

### 5.1 Inspect the Edit Grid  

- **Blobs** should appear as clean, continuous shapes that follow the vocal melody.  
- **Loudness** (color shading) should correspond to the vocal dynamics you set during gain staging.  
- **Formant** markers (if visible) should be stable; erratic shifts could indicate a detection error.

### 5.2 Play Back with the Transport  

Press **Spacebar** to start playback. While listening, watch the **Playhead** (horizontal axis) move across the Edit Grid. Confirm that:

- The **Pitch‑Draw** cursor follows the vocal line without jumping.  
- No **ghost notes** appear in polyphonic mode (if you chose monophonic).  

If you notice mismatches, repeat the detection step after adjusting the **Detection Sensitivity** slider in the Inspector.

### 5.3 Save a “Ready‑to‑Edit” Session  

Before moving on to pitch correction, save the Melodyne project:

1. **File → Save As…**  
2. Name it with the song title and “_Prep” suffix (e.g., *SongName_Vocal_Prep.mel*).  

This creates a checkpoint you can return to if later edits introduce unwanted artifacts.

---

## 6. Workflow Checklist  

| Step | Action | Why It Matters |
|------|--------|----------------|
| **1** | Export vocal at 44.1 kHz/48 kHz, 24 bit (or higher) | Preserves timing and dynamic detail |
| **2** | Use WAV/AIFF; avoid lossy codecs | Prevents pre‑existing compression artifacts |
| **3** | Consolidate takes into a single file | Guarantees continuity for detection |
| **4** | Import into Melodyne; confirm sample rate | Avoids resampling errors |
| **5** | Choose **Monophonic** or **Polyphonic** based on material | Ensures accurate pitch blobs |
| **6** | Normalize to –6 dBFS; set RMS around –18 dBFS | Provides headroom for amplitude edits |
| **7** | Apply noise gate or spectral reducer if needed | Improves detection reliability |
| **8** | Verify Edit Grid for clean blobs and correct loudness | Confirms readiness for pitch editing |
| **9** | Save a “prepared” project file | Enables safe return point |

Running through this checklist before you ever touch the **Pitch‑Draw** tool guarantees that the Edit Grid you’ll later manipulate is a faithful representation of the original performance.

---

## 7. Real‑World Example: From Rough Take to Ready‑to‑Edit  

> **Scenario:** A pop vocalist recorded a lead in a home studio using a condenser mic and a portable audio interface at 48 kHz/24 bit. The track includes a faint fan noise and a slight gain boost in the chorus.

1. **Export:** Bounced the track as a 48 kHz/24 bit WAV, preserving the full dynamic range.  
2. **Noise Reduction:** Applied a light spectral reduction (‑12 dB) to the fan hum, then re‑exported.  
3. **Gain Staging:** Normalized the file to –6 dBFS, then set the RMS to –17 dBFS for a balanced level.  
4. **Import:** Opened the cleaned file in Melodyne Editor, confirmed the sample rate, and selected **Monophonic** detection.  
5. **Verification:** The Edit Grid displayed smooth, continuous blobs with no ghost notes. The **Spectrogram** showed the fan noise removed, and the **Amplitude** shading matched the vocal’s natural dynamics.  

With the track now pre‑processed, the subsequent pitch‑correction steps (covered in Chapter 4) proceeded without any audible artifacts, even after heavy quantisation to the nearest semitone.

---

## 8. Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them  

| Pitfall | Symptom | Remedy |
|---------|---------|--------|
| **Mismatched sample rates** | Pitch drift or timing jitter when playing back | Re‑export the vocal at the DAW’s sample rate and re‑import |
| **Using Polyphonic on a solo vocal** | Excessive blobs, “ghost” notes, slower detection | Switch to **Monophonic**, re‑detect |
| **Over‑normalizing** | Clipping in peaks, loss of dynamic nuance | Normalize to –6 dBFS, then manually adjust RMS |
| **Skipping noise reduction** | Detection errors in quiet sections, erratic blobs | Apply a gentle noise gate or spectral reducer before import |
| **Ignoring the Spectrogram** | Hidden clicks or rumble that cause pitch‑shift artifacts | Scan the spectrogram and edit problematic frequencies pre‑emptively |

---

## 9. Preparing Multiple Vocal Tracks  

When a project contains **lead, harmony, and background vocals**, repeat the above workflow for each track individually. Keeping each vocal on its own **Melodyne instance** with appropriate detection modes (lead = Monophonic, harmonies = Polyphonic if layered) ensures clean editing later on.  

If you plan to **export stems** from Melodyne, label each instance clearly (e.g., “Lead‑Prep”, “Harmony‑1‑Prep”) to avoid confusion during the mixing stage.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Export at native resolution** (44.1 kHz/48 kHz, 24 bit or higher) to preserve timing and dynamics.  
- **Choose the detection algorithm** that matches the vocal material: Monophonic for solo lines, Polyphonic for dense arrangements.  
- **Gain‑stage early**: normalize to –6 dBFS and set RMS around –18 dBFS for optimal headroom.  
- **Apply noise reduction** before detection to prevent artifacts that confuse Melodyne’s algorithms.  
- **Verify the Edit Grid** (clean blobs, correct loudness, stable formants) before moving on to pitch editing.  
- Use the **pre‑processing checklist** to ensure each vocal track is ready for precise, artifact‑free pitch correction.

modules.title: Basic Pitch Editing in Melodic Mode
modules.content:
## Getting Started: A Real‑World Example

Imagine you’ve just finished tracking the lead vocal for a pop ballad. The performance is emotionally convincing, but a few phrases sit a half‑step flat, and the climactic high note drifts sharp by about 30 cents. The rest of the arrangement is already mixed, so you need a quick, transparent fix that keeps the singer’s natural timbre intact.  

In **Melodic mode**, the solution is as simple as selecting the offending pitch blobs, snapping them to the correct scale degree, and nudging the formant just enough to preserve the vocal’s character. The steps below walk you through that exact workflow, using the tools you’ve already seen in *Introduction to Melodyne Interface and Workflow* and *Core Pitch Correction Concepts*.

---

## Selecting and Moving Pitch Blobs

### 1. Identify the target notes  

- Switch to the **Edit Grid** (if it isn’t already visible) via the **Tool Bar**.  
- Zoom in on the phrase in question; the **Horizontal Axis (Time)** lets you see the exact location of each note, while the **Vertical Axis (Pitch)** displays the blobs.  
- Use the **Amplitude view** (toggle in the Inspector) to differentiate voiced sections from breathy or silent parts—this helps avoid moving stray, low‑amplitude blobs that could introduce artifacts.

### 2. Make a selection  

| Method | When to use it |
|--------|----------------|
| **Click‑drag** a rectangle around a group of blobs | Quick selection of a phrase or a series of notes |
| **Shift‑click** individual blobs | Fine‑tuning when only a few notes need adjustment |
| **Lasso (Ctrl + drag)** | Irregular shapes, e.g., when a vibrato tail extends beyond the main note |

> **Tip:** The **Select** tool (shortcut **S**) stays active until you click another tool, so you can freely move between selection and editing without re‑clicking the toolbar.

### 3. Move the blobs  

- **Mouse drag:** Click any selected blob and drag vertically toward the desired pitch.  
- **Arrow keys:** With a blob selected, press **↑** or **↓** to move in 1‑cent increments; hold **Shift** for 10‑cent steps.  
- **Snap to nearest note:** Enable **Snap to Scale** (Inspector → *Snap* → *Scale*). When active, any vertical movement automatically snaps to the nearest note in the chosen scale, eliminating the need to guess the exact pitch value.

> **Pro tip:** If the track is in a key that changes mid‑song, open the **Scale** dropdown and select **Custom**, then draw a temporary key change line to guide the snapping for that section.

---

## Using the Pitch Tool

The **Pitch‑Draw** tool is the workhorse for precise pitch manipulation. While the **Select** tool lets you move whole blobs, **Pitch‑Draw** lets you reshape the pitch contour inside a single blob, perfect for correcting subtle intonation errors without destroying natural vibrato.

### Activating the Tool  

- Click the **Pitch‑Draw** icon on the **Tool Bar**, or press **P**. The cursor changes to a pencil‑like shape, indicating you’re in draw mode.

### Editing a blob  

1. **Hover** over the target blob; a small tooltip shows its current pitch (e.g., *C4 + 85 cents*).  
2. **Click‑drag** upward or downward to raise or lower the pitch. The pitch curve updates in real time, and the **Note editor** (opened by double‑clicking the blob) reflects the new value.  
3. **Fine‑tune** with the **Keyboard nudging** (↑/↓) while the cursor is over the blob. This is especially handy for micro‑adjustments under 10 cents.

### Controlling the draw behavior  

- **Snap to Scale** (still active from the previous step) forces every drawn point to land on a scale degree, ensuring melodic consistency.  
- **Quantize** (Inspector → *Quantize*) can be toggled on to force the entire blob to the nearest semitone automatically after you finish drawing. Use this sparingly; a little natural variation often sounds more musical than a perfectly quantized line.

> **Note:** The **Pitch‑Draw** tool works on the **Vertical Axis** only; horizontal movement (time) is handled by the **Time‑Stretch** or **Loop** tools, which you’ll explore later.

---

## The Correct Pitch Function

While the **Pitch‑Draw** tool offers granular control, the **Correct Pitch** function provides a rapid, “one‑click” solution for notes that are simply out of tune. It’s especially useful for the scenario described at the start of this chapter.

### Accessing the function  

- Select one or more blobs with the **Select** tool.  
- In the **Inspector**, locate the **Correct Pitch** button (often displayed as a small arrow pointing to a musical staff).  
- Alternatively, right‑click the selection and choose **Correct Pitch** from the context menu.

### Options inside the dialog  

| Option | Description |
|--------|-------------|
| **Target Scale** | Choose *Major*, *Minor*, *Custom*, or *Chromatic*. The function will snap each selected blob to the nearest note within this scale. |
| **Strength** | Slider from 0 % (no change) to 100 % (full snap). A value around 70 % usually yields a natural‑sounding correction while retaining expressive nuances. |
| **Formant Preservation** | Checkbox that, when enabled, automatically adjusts the **Formant** slider to keep timbre consistent after pitch correction. |
| **Lock to Original Rhythm** | Ensures the timing of the notes stays untouched while pitch is altered. |

### Applying the correction  

1. Click **Apply**. Melodyne instantly repositions the selected blobs.  
2. Play back the segment (Spacebar) to hear the result.  
3. If the correction feels too aggressive, undo (**Ctrl + Z**) and lower the **Strength** slider, then re‑apply.

> **Tip:** For vocal tracks, a **Strength** of 80 % combined with **Formant Preservation** turned on usually gives a transparent result. Adjust as needed based on the singer’s vocal style.

---

## Simple Formant Preservation

Formant shifting is the secret behind keeping a vocal sounding “human” after pitch changes. When you raise a note, the vocal tract’s resonant frequencies (formants) should rise proportionally; otherwise the voice can sound thin or “chipmunk‑like.”

### Why a simple approach works  

In this chapter we’ll use **Melodyne’s built‑in formant lock**, which automatically links the formant to the pitch shift. It’s a **single‑click** solution that works for most corrective tasks, leaving the more advanced DNA‑based control for later chapters.

### Enabling formant preservation  

- After moving a blob (via **Select**, **Pitch‑Draw**, or **Correct Pitch**), open the **Note editor** by double‑clicking the blob.  
- Locate the **Formant** slider (usually below the pitch display).  
- Click the **link icon** (looks like a chain) to enable **Formant Preservation**. When the link is active, any further pitch movement automatically updates the formant proportionally.  

### Quick check for naturalness  

1. **Solo** the vocal track and listen to the corrected note in isolation.  
2. Toggle the **Formant** lock off temporarily; if the voice sounds thin or overly bright, the lock is doing its job.  
3. If the timbre still feels off, nudge the **Formant** slider manually in small increments (±5 cents) while the note is still selected.

> **Caution:** Over‑adjusting formants can introduce “nasal” or “hollow” artifacts. The goal is subtlety—aim for the smallest movement that restores naturalness.

---

## Workflow: From Identification to Correction

Putting the tools together into a repeatable process speeds up editing and reduces fatigue. Below is a **step‑by‑step workflow** you can follow for any vocal phrase that needs pitch polishing.

1. **Load the track** and ensure **Melodic mode** is active (already covered in *Preparing and Importing Vocal Tracks*).  
2. **Activate Snap to Scale** in the Inspector, selecting the appropriate key or custom scale.  
3. **Scan the Edit Grid** using the **Transport** controls (Play/Stop) to locate problem notes.  
4. **Select** the offending blobs (click‑drag or lasso).  
5. **Choose the correction method:**  
   - For isolated, clearly off‑key notes → use **Correct Pitch** with 70‑80 % strength.  
   - For notes that need subtle shaping (e.g., a slightly flat vibrato tail) → use **Pitch‑Draw**.  
6. **Enable Formant Preservation** in the Note editor (or check the box in the Correct Pitch dialog).  
7. **Listen** to the corrected segment. If any artifact appears, undo and adjust **Strength** or **Formant** manually.  
8. **Repeat** until the entire phrase sits comfortably within the intended scale.  

> **Pro tip:** Use the **Loop** function (Inspector → *Loop*) to isolate a short segment while you work, preventing accidental edits elsewhere.

---

## Common Pitfalls and Quick Fixes

Even with a solid workflow, it’s easy to stumble into typical issues. Below are the most frequent mistakes and how to resolve them quickly.

| Pitfall | Why it Happens | Quick Fix |
|---------|----------------|-----------|
| **Over‑snapping** – notes sound robotic | Using 100 % strength or disabling formant lock | Reduce **Strength** to 60‑80 % and re‑enable formant preservation |
| **Moving silent blobs** – introduces clicks | Selecting a large rectangle that includes low‑amplitude regions | Toggle **Amplitude view** and deselect any blobs below a visible threshold |
| **Unintended pitch drift** – vibrato gets flattened | Dragging an entire blob without checking the internal curve | Double‑click the blob, view the **Pitch‑Draw** curve, and restore natural vibrato with subtle hand‑drawn adjustments |
| **Formant mismatch** – voice sounds thin after upward correction | Formant lock disabled or manual formant shift too far | Re‑enable formant link, then fine‑tune the slider in ±5 cents increments |
| **Scale mismatch** – notes snap to the wrong key | Wrong scale selected in **Snap to Scale** dropdown | Double‑check the key signature in the Inspector and adjust the scale accordingly |

---

## Practice Exercise

> **Scenario:** A male vocalist sings a verse in A‑minor. The second line contains three problematic notes: the 2nd beat is flat by ~40 cents, the 4th beat is sharp by ~25 cents, and the final held note drifts upward by ~30 cents.  
> **Goal:** Correct the three notes using the techniques covered, preserving the singer’s timbre.

**Steps**

1. **Enable Snap to Scale → A‑minor**.  
2. **Zoom** into the second line; use **Amplitude view** to isolate the three notes.  
3. **Select** the first problematic blob (flat note).  
4. Open the **Correct Pitch** dialog, set **Strength** to **75 %**, tick **Formant Preservation**, and click **Apply**.  
5. **Select** the second blob (sharp note). This time, use **Pitch‑Draw**: click‑drag the point down by ~20 cents, ensuring the curve stays smooth.  
6. **Select** the final held note. Because it’s a long sustain, use **Correct Pitch** again, but set **Strength** to **80 %** for a firmer correction.  
7. **Play back** the entire line. If the final note sounds thin, double‑click the blob, enable the **Formant link**, and nudge the **Formant** slider up by 5 cents.  
8. **Loop** the line and listen repeatedly until the pitch feels natural and in key.

When you’re satisfied, **save** the Melodyne project and **export** the corrected audio (refer to *Integration, Export, and Best Practices* for the final steps).

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Select** the exact blobs you need to edit—use click‑drag, shift‑click, or lasso, and always verify with the **Amplitude view**.  
- **Snap to Scale** automatically aligns moved blobs with the correct musical pitch, reducing guesswork.  
- The **Pitch‑Draw** tool lets you sculpt pitch contours inside a single blob for subtle, expressive corrections.  
- **Correct Pitch** offers a fast, strength‑controlled snap to the nearest scale degree; combine it with **Formant Preservation** for transparent results.  
- Simple formant control—via the **Formant link** in the Note editor—maintains vocal timbre after pitch shifts without needing advanced DNA editing.  
- A repeatable workflow (identify → select → correct → listen → fine‑tune) keeps you efficient and prevents over‑processing.  

By mastering these fundamental techniques, you’ll be able to clean up off‑key vocal performances quickly while preserving the natural character that makes each singer unique.

modules.title: Advanced Pitch Editing – DNA and Formant Control
modules.content:
## When “Perfect Pitch” Means “Perfectly Natural”

Imagine you’ve just recorded a soulful R&B vocal line. The singer’s phrasing is spot‑on, the emotion is raw, but a few notes sit just a half‑step flat, and the high‑end feels a little thin. You reach for Melody DNA, not to yank the notes into a robotic grid, but to **nudge each pitch at the micro‑tonal level while keeping the singer’s unique timbre intact**. This is the sweet spot where advanced DNA editing meets independent formant control, and it’s the difference between a polished performance and a synthetic‑sounding impersonation.

---

## Activating DNA Mode

1. **Open the Edit Grid** – If you’ve followed *Preparing and Importing Vocal Tracks*, your track should already be displayed in the Edit Grid with the usual horizontal (time) and vertical (pitch) axes.
2. **Switch to DNA** – In the Tool Bar, click the **DNA** button (or press **Shift + D**). The interface will change from the “blob” view to a series of **note‑level markers** that can be expanded.
3. **Expand the DNA View** – Hover over a note and press **Ctrl + ↑** (or click the small “+” beside the note name) to reveal the underlying **pitch‑curve points**. You’ll now see a dense set of draggable dots representing the raw pitch data extracted from the audio.

> **Tip:** If the DNA markers appear “frozen,” make sure **“Show DNA”** is enabled in the Inspector panel. This option was introduced in *Core Pitch Correction Concepts* and must be toggled on for detailed editing.

---

## Micro‑tonal Pitch Editing

### Why Micro‑tonal Matters

Even after quantizing a vocal to a scale, the **natural intonation** of a singer often contains subtle bends that give a performance its character. Over‑quantizing can flatten these nuances, turning a warm vocal into a sterile tone‑row. DNA lets you **edit at the cent level**—the smallest pitch unit Melodyne can manipulate.

### Editing Workflow

1. **Select a Note Segment**  
   - Use the **Select** tool (shortcut **S**) to draw a region around the pitch segment you want to adjust.  
   - The selected area will highlight the underlying pitch‑curve points.

2. **Zoom for Precision**  
   - Press **Ctrl + Mouse Wheel** or use the **Zoom** slider in the Transport panel to get a close‑up view.  
   - At 400 % zoom, each dot corresponds roughly to a single cent of pitch movement.

3. **Nudge with Pitch‑Draw**  
   - Activate **Pitch‑Draw** (shortcut **P**) and click‑drag a line across the selected points.  
   - The cursor snaps to the nearest cent, and a small tooltip shows the exact **cents** value as you draw.

4. **Fine‑Tune with Keyboard**  
   - With the points selected, use the **arrow keys** to move them **±1 cent** per press. Holding **Shift** speeds it up to **±5 cents**.  
   - This is ideal for making minute corrections without disturbing neighboring points.

5. **Listen in Context**  
   - Toggle **Loop** (shortcut **L**) to audition the edited segment repeatedly.  
   - Use the **Transport** playback controls to compare before/after by enabling **A/B** mode (click the **A/B** button in the Toolbar).

### Practical Example

> **Scenario:** A lead vocal line lands on a G4 that is consistently 30 cents flat during the chorus.  
> **Solution:**  
> - Expand DNA for the G4 note.  
> - Select the flat portion (the first half of the note).  
> - With Pitch‑Draw, raise the curve by **+30 cents**.  
> - Apply a subtle **fade‑in** to the correction so the transition feels natural.  

---

## Independent Formant Manipulation

### Understanding Formant vs. Pitch

Formants are resonant frequencies that shape the **perceived timbre** of a voice. In *Basic Pitch Editing in Melodic Mode*, you learned that moving a note up or down also drags its formant, often resulting in the classic “chipmunk” effect. DNA decouples these parameters, allowing you to **shift pitch while leaving formants untouched—or vice‑versa**.

### Adjusting Formant Independently

1. **Open the Formant Editor**  
   - With a note selected, click the **Formant** tab in the Inspector (next to Pitch, Amplitude, etc.).  
   - A horizontal slider appears, showing the current formant offset in **semitones**.

2. **Lock or Unlock Formants**  
   - By default, the **“Link Pitch & Formant”** icon (a chain link) is active. Click it to **unlock** the two parameters.  
   - When unlocked, moving the pitch curve no longer affects the formant slider.

3. **Shift Formants Separately**  
   - Drag the Formant slider left or right to lower or raise the timbre.  
   - For micro‑tonal adjustments, hold **Alt** while dragging; a numeric readout appears, letting you set the offset to the exact **cent** value.

4. **Preserve Naturalness**  
   - Small formant shifts (≤ ± 15 cents) are generally imperceptible and can correct “thin” high notes without sounding artificial.  
   - Larger shifts should be applied sparingly and often benefit from a **smooth automation curve** rather than a hard step.

### Real‑World Use Cases

| Situation | Desired Outcome | Formant Adjustment |
|-----------|----------------|-------------------|
| High‑note sounding thin | Add warmth | Raise formant by **+10 cents** |
| Low‑end sounding muddy | Increase clarity | Lower formant by **‑12 cents** |
| Double‑track harmonies | Match timbre | Align formant of the harmony to the lead (copy formant value) |

> **Tip:** Use the **Copy/Paste Formant** command (right‑click on the Formant field) to transfer a desirable formant setting from one note to another, ensuring consistent timbre across a phrase.

---

## Pitch Drift & Vibrato Tools for Expressive Fine‑Tuning

### What Is Pitch Drift?

Pitch drift refers to a **slow, intentional shift** in pitch over the duration of a note—think of a singer subtly sliding up at the end of a phrase. Melodyne’s **Pitch Drift** tool (found under the **Pitch** tab in the Inspector) lets you replicate or correct this behavior.

#### Using Pitch Drift

1. **Enable Drift Mode** – Click the **Pitch Drift** button (looks like a slanted line) while a note is selected.  
2. **Set Start/End Values** – In the Inspector, enter the **start** and **end** pitch offsets in cents.  
3. **Apply Curve** – The pitch curve will automatically generate a linear drift between the two values.  
4. **Adjust Curve Shape** – Switch to **Pitch‑Draw** and reshape the drift if you want a non‑linear glide (e.g., exponential or logarithmic).

### Refining Vibrato

Vibrato is a rapid, periodic pitch modulation that adds life to a vocal line. While *Core Pitch Correction Concepts* covered basic vibrato detection, DNA lets you **edit each vibrato cycle**.

1. **Detect Vibrato** – With DNA expanded, Melodyne automatically flags vibrato cycles with small **wiggle markers** on the pitch curve.  
2. **Select a Cycle** – Click a wiggle marker to highlight the underlying points.  
3. **Modify Depth & Rate**  
   - In the **Vibrato** section of the Inspector, adjust the **Depth** (cents) and **Rate** (Hz).  
   - For micro‑tonal tweaking, keep depth changes under **±5 cents** to avoid sounding mechanical.  
4. **Smooth Transitions** – Use the **Amplitude** tool to fade vibrato in or out, ensuring the modulation starts and ends naturally.

### Combining Drift & Vibrato

A common scenario is a **slow upward drift** that culminates in a **final vibrato burst**. To achieve this:

- Apply **Pitch Drift** to the note’s main body.  
- Near the note’s tail, enable **Vibrato** and increase its **Depth** while reducing the **Rate** for a wider, more expressive wobble.  
- Listen in loop mode and adjust until the transition feels seamless.

---

## Workflow Blueprint: From Raw Take to Polished Vocal

Below is a step‑by‑step checklist that integrates the techniques discussed. Feel free to adapt the order to suit your workflow.

1. **Initial DNA Activation**  
   - Open the Edit Grid → enable DNA → expand notes you intend to edit.

2. **Micro‑tonal Pitch Corrections**  
   - Select problem sections → zoom → use Pitch‑Draw or arrow‑key nudging → A/B audition.

3. **Formant Preservation**  
   - Unlock Pitch‑Formant link → verify formant values remain unchanged after pitch moves.  
   - If a note sounds thin, apply a subtle formant lift; if it sounds nasal, apply a slight drop.

4. **Apply Pitch Drift (if needed)**  
   - Enable Pitch Drift → set start/end offsets → reshape curve for natural glide.

5. **Refine Vibrato**  
   - Locate vibrato cycles → adjust depth/rate → smooth with Amplitude fade.

6. **Global Consistency Check**  
   - Solo the vocal track → enable **Loop** over the entire phrase → toggle **A/B** to compare with the original.  
   - Use the **Inspector’s** loudness meter to ensure no unintended volume changes occurred during pitch/formant edits.

7. **Render & Export**  
   - Once satisfied, bounce the track (or export stems) as described in *Integration, Export, and Best Practices* (later chapter).  

> **Pro Tip:** Keep a **duplicate** of the original audio track hidden in the project. If you ever need to revert a DNA edit, you can quickly copy the original waveform back into the Edit Grid.

---

## Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them

| Pitfall | Symptom | Remedy |
|---------|---------|--------|
| **Formant “Chipmunk” Effect** | Pitch raised, timbre becomes unnaturally bright | Ensure the **Link Pitch & Formant** icon is **unlocked** before adjusting pitch. |
| **Over‑Quantized Vibrato** | Vibrato sounds mechanical, lacking organic variation | Reduce vibrato **Depth** to ≤ ±5 cents; manually reshape the curve for subtle irregularities. |
| **Pitch Drift Too Steep** | Note sounds like a slide rather than a natural glide | Lower the **End Offset** value; apply a smoother curve (e.g., exponential) via Pitch‑Draw. |
| **Unintended Loudness Changes** | Certain notes become noticeably louder after editing | After pitch/formant changes, check the **Amplitude** curve; adjust with the **Amplitude** tool to even out levels. |

---

## Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

- **Activate DNA:** Toolbar → DNA (⇧ D)  
- **Expand a Note:** Ctrl + ↑ (or click “+” beside note name)  
- **Micro‑tonal Nudge:** Arrow keys (±1 cent) / Shift + Arrow (±5 cents)  
- **Unlock Pitch/Formant:** Click chain‑link icon in Inspector  
- **Formant Shift:** Formant slider (hold Alt for cent precision)  
- **Pitch Drift:** Pitch → Pitch Drift → set start/end offsets  
- **Vibrato Edit:** Select wiggle marker → Vibrato panel → adjust Depth/Rate  
- **Loop Playback:** L (or click Loop button)  
- **A/B Comparison:** Click A/B button in Toolbar  

---

## ## Key Takeaways

- **DNA mode unlocks the raw pitch data**, letting you edit at the cent level without sacrificing musicality.  
- **Formant and pitch are independent** once the link is unlocked; adjust one without affecting the other to avoid “chipmunk” artifacts.  
- **Pitch Drift** creates natural‑sounding slides, while **Vibrato tools** let you fine‑tune expressive modulation.  
- A disciplined workflow—activate DNA, correct micro‑tonal errors, preserve formants, apply drift/vibrato, then A/B test—yields professional, natural vocal results.  

By mastering these DNA and formant controls, you’ll transform almost‑perfect vocal takes into truly polished performances while keeping the singer’s unique character front and center.

modules.title: Polyphonic Mode for Complex Vocal Arrangements
modules.content:
## When a Four‑Part Harmony Collides with a Mic

Imagine you’re mixing a studio recording of a pop‑rock anthem. The lead vocalist has recorded a tight double‑track, while the backing choir was captured in a single take. In the chorus, the choir’s Soprano, Alto, Tenor, and Bass parts overlap so heavily that the waveform looks like a single, dense wall of sound. When you load the track into Melodyne, the Edit Grid shows a tangled forest of blobs—some clearly belonging to the lead, others to the choir, and a few that are a blend of two or three voices.  

Your goal is simple: **pull each individual note out, fix any pitch drift, and keep the lush blend intact**. This is exactly what Polyphonic mode was built for. In the sections that follow we’ll walk through a practical workflow that meets the three learning objectives:

1. Detect and separate overlapping notes within a polyphonic vocal segment.  
2. Edit individual note blobs without affecting adjacent pitches.  
3. Correct the tuning of stacked harmonies while preserving the overall blend.

All of the tools you need—**Edit Grid, Tool Bar, Inspector, Pitch‑Draw, Quantize**, and the **Polyphonic algorithm**—have already been introduced in earlier chapters. We’ll now focus on how they work together in a real‑world, multi‑voice scenario.

---

## 1. Setting Up Polyphonic Mode

### 1.1 Choose the Right Algorithm

When you first drag the vocal file onto a new track, Melodyne defaults to **Monophonic** detection. Switch to **Polyphonic** by clicking the **Algorithm** selector in the Inspector (see Chapter 1).  

> **Tip:** If you’re unsure whether a segment is truly polyphonic, enable **“Show Detection Confidence”** in the Inspector. Low confidence values usually indicate overlapping notes that need manual refinement.

### 1.2 Define the Analysis Window

Polyphonic detection works best when the analysis window matches the density of the material:

1. **Zoom in** on the Edit Grid until you can see individual note blobs clearly (use the **Horizontal Axis** zoom).  
2. In the Inspector, set **“Maximum Polyphony”** to a number slightly higher than the expected number of simultaneous voices (e.g., 5 for a four‑part choir plus lead double‑track).  
3. Click **Analyze**. Melodyne will now parse the audio, creating a separate blob for each detected pitch.

> **Caution:** Over‑estimating polyphony can cause the algorithm to split a single note into multiple blobs, creating “ghost” notes that must be cleaned up later.

---

## 2. Detecting Overlapping Notes

### 2.1 Visual Clues in the Edit Grid

In Polyphonic mode, overlapping notes appear as **stacked blobs** that share the same time axis but occupy different vertical positions. A quick visual scan can reveal:

- **Dense clusters** where three or more blobs sit within a few milliseconds.  
- **Irregular blob shapes** (elongated or wavy) that often indicate a note transitioning into another voice.

### 2.2 Using the **“Note Separation”** Tool

The **Note Separation** tool (found on the Tool Bar) lets you manually split blobs that the algorithm merged:

1. Select the problematic blob.  
2. Click the **Note Separation** icon.  
3. Drag the split line vertically to the point where you want the notes to divide.  
4. Release the mouse; Melodyne will create two distinct blobs.

> **Pro Tip:** Hold **Shift** while dragging to constrain the split to perfect vertical or horizontal lines, which helps maintain pitch accuracy.

### 2.3 Verifying with the **“Audio Preview”**

After each split, press the **Spacebar** (or click the **Play** button) to hear the isolated notes. The **Audio Preview** window will highlight the currently selected blob, letting you confirm whether the separation sounds natural.

---

## 3. Editing Individual Blobs Without Collateral Damage

Now that each voice is represented by its own blob, you can edit them independently. The key is to keep the **selection context** tight.

### 3.1 Isolate a Single Blob

1. Click on the desired blob.  
2. In the Inspector, enable **“Solo Blob”** (the small headphone icon). This mutes all other blobs, ensuring you hear only the note you’re about to edit.

### 3.2 Pitch‑Draw for Precise Corrections

With the blob selected:

1. Switch to **Pitch‑Draw** (Tool Bar).  
2. Click and drag the pitch curve to correct any drift.  
   - **Fine‑tune** by holding **Alt** (or **Option** on Mac) to snap to the nearest cent.  
   - **Snap to scale** by enabling **“Quantize to Scale”** in the Inspector (you’ll set the scale later).

> **Note:** Because you’re in Polyphonic mode, moving one blob’s pitch does **not** affect neighboring blobs, even if they overlap in time. This is the core advantage over Melodic mode for dense harmonies.

### 3.3 Adjusting Amplitude and Formant

While the blob remains soloed:

- **Amplitude**: Drag the vertical bar in the Inspector to balance the voice level within the chord.  
- **Formant**: Use the **Formant** slider to retain the natural timbre of each singer. Small adjustments (±5–10 %) often prevent the “chipmunk” effect that can appear when pitch‑shifting large intervals.

### 3.4 Locking Changes

After you’re satisfied, click the **Lock** icon in the Inspector. Locked blobs protect your edits from accidental changes when you move on to the next voice.

---

## 4. Tuning Stacked Harmonies While Preserving Blend

With each voice isolated, the next step is to bring the entire chord into accurate tuning. This is where **Quantize** and **Scale Detection** shine—though the latter will be explored in detail later, a brief look‑ahead helps illustrate the workflow.

### 4.1 Establish a Reference Scale

Even though full scale detection belongs to Chapter 7, you can manually define the key for the current section:

1. Open the **Scale** dropdown in the Inspector.  
2. Choose the appropriate key (e.g., **C major**).  
3. Enable **“Quantize to Scale”**.

Now any pitch adjustments you make with Pitch‑Draw will automatically snap to the nearest scale degree, keeping the chord harmonically consistent.

### 4.2 Quantize the Whole Chord

Instead of editing each note individually, you can apply a **global quantization** to the entire harmonic cluster:

1. **Select all blobs** belonging to the chord (drag a selection box across the cluster).  
2. In the Inspector, set the **Quantize Strength** slider to 50 % for a gentle pull, or 100 % for a hard snap.  
3. Click **Apply**.

> **Result:** Each note moves to the nearest pitch that fits the selected scale, while the relative timing and formant remain untouched. Because the selection is limited to the chord, adjacent chords are unaffected.

### 4.3 Fine‑Tuning the Blend

After quantization, listen to the chord as a whole:

- If the blend sounds **thin** or **phase‑y**, adjust the **Amplitude** of the individual blobs to restore balance.  
- Use the **Formant** sliders to subtly shift the timbral character of each voice, ensuring the choir still sounds cohesive.

> **Tip:** A quick **“A‑B”** comparison (toggle the **Bypass** button) helps you judge whether the tuning changes improved the musicality without sacrificing the natural blend.

---

## 5. Practical Workflow: From Messy Take to Polished Harmony

Below is a step‑by‑step checklist you can follow on any polyphonic vocal track. Feel free to adapt the order to suit your own workflow.

| Step | Action | Tool / Setting |
|------|--------|----------------|
| 1 | Load the vocal file and switch to **Polyphonic** mode. | Inspector → Algorithm |
| 2 | Set **Maximum Polyphony** to one higher than the expected number of simultaneous voices. | Inspector |
| 3 | Run **Analyze** and review the detection confidence. | Inspector |
| 4 | Identify dense clusters and use **Note Separation** to split merged blobs. | Tool Bar → Note Separation |
| 5 | Solo each blob, then correct pitch with **Pitch‑Draw**. | Tool Bar → Pitch‑Draw; Inspector → Solo Blob |
| 6 | Adjust **Amplitude** and **Formant** to maintain blend. | Inspector |
| 7 | Lock edited blobs. | Inspector → Lock |
| 8 | Define the chord’s key and enable **Quantize to Scale**. | Inspector → Scale |
| 9 | Select the entire chord and apply **Quantize** (adjust strength as needed). | Inspector |
|10 | Perform a final **A‑B** check, tweak any remaining amplitude/formant imbalances. | Bypass button; Inspector |
|11 | Export or bounce the corrected track. | DAW export function |

### Real‑World Example: “Echoes of Summer”

In a recent session, a client recorded a choir on a single mic in a reverberant hall. The initial Melodyne analysis produced 12 blobs for a single chord, many of which were ghost notes. By applying the workflow above:

- **Note Separation** reduced the blob count from 12 to 5, matching the actual number of singers.  
- **Pitch‑Draw** corrected a 30‑cent drift in the Tenor line that was otherwise masked by the surrounding voices.  
- **Quantize** to the song’s **G major** key brought the whole chord within 5 cents of perfect tuning.  
- Minimal **Formant** tweaks (±4 %) restored the natural choir warmth that had been dulled by the initial pitch correction.

The final mix retained the lush, organic feel of the live recording while eliminating the subtle intonation issues that would have been impossible to hear without visual analysis.

---

## 6. Common Pitfalls & How to Avoid Them

| Pitfall | Symptom | Remedy |
|---------|---------|--------|
| **Over‑splitting notes** | Too many tiny blobs; unnatural “stutter” when playing back. | Use **Maximum Polyphony** wisely; after splitting, consolidate any stray fragments with **Merge Blobs** (right‑click → Merge). |
| **Quantizing too aggressively** | Chord sounds mechanical; timbre becomes thin. | Reduce **Quantize Strength** to 30–50 % and manually fine‑tune outliers with **Pitch‑Draw**. |
| **Neglecting formant when shifting large intervals** | Voices sound “chipmunked” or “distant.” | Always enable **Formant** control; make small formant adjustments after major pitch changes. |
| **Editing while multiple blobs are selected** | Unintended changes to neighboring notes. | Double‑check the selection box; use **Solo Blob** to isolate the target before editing. |
| **Ignoring detection confidence** | Missed notes or ghost notes remain hidden. | Review the confidence overlay; manually add or delete blobs where confidence is low (< 70 %). |

---

## 7. Extending Polyphonic Editing to Other Sources

While this chapter focuses on vocal harmonies, the same techniques apply to:

- **String sections** recorded with a single mic (e.g., violins + violas).  
- **Synth pads** built from layered oscillators that create chordal textures.  
- **Hybrid vocal‑instrument blends** (e.g., a singer plus a vocoder layer).

The key is always to **match the polyphony setting** to the actual number of simultaneous sources and to **validate the detection** visually and aurally before committing to edits.

---

## 8. Quick Reference Cheat Sheet

- **Algorithm → Polyphonic** – Switches detection mode.  
- **Maximum Polyphony** – Controls how many simultaneous notes Melodyne will try to extract.  
- **Note Separation** – Split merged blobs vertically.  
- **Solo Blob** – Mutes all other notes for focused editing.  
- **Pitch‑Draw** – Freehand pitch correction; holds pitch while moving.  
- **Quantize to Scale** – Snap notes to a defined key; adjust **Strength** for subtlety.  
- **Lock** – Protects edited blobs from later changes.  
- **A‑B Toggle (Bypass)** – Compare original vs. corrected audio instantly.

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Polyphonic mode** lets you isolate and edit individual notes even when several voices overlap in time.  
- Use **Maximum Polyphony** and **Detection Confidence** to ensure accurate initial analysis.  
- **Note Separation** and **Solo Blob** are essential for cleanly splitting and editing overlapping notes without affecting neighboring pitches.  
- **Pitch‑Draw**, **Amplitude**, and **Formant** controls allow precise, voice‑specific adjustments while preserving the natural blend of stacked harmonies.  
- **Quantize to Scale** (with adjustable strength) aligns entire chords to the correct key, but always follow up with subtle manual tweaks to avoid a mechanical sound.  
- Regular **A‑B checks** and careful management of **Selection** prevent unintended collateral edits.  

By mastering these steps, you can transform dense, multi‑voice vocal recordings into pitch‑perfect, harmonically rich performances—all while keeping the organic character that makes choral and layered vocal arrangements so compelling.

modules.title: Using Scale and Chord Detection for Musical Accuracy
modules.content:
## Setting the Harmonic Context in Melodyne  

Before any pitch‑correction can be musically sensible, Melodyne needs to know *what* it is correcting. The **Inspector** panel houses the **Key**, **Scale**, and **Chord Progression** controls that define the harmonic backdrop for every blob on the **Edit Grid**.  

1. **Open the Inspector** – If it’s hidden, click the “i” icon on the **Tool Bar**.  
2. **Select the correct Key** – Click the key signature dropdown and choose the tonic (e.g., **C‑major**).  
3. **Choose a Scale** – Melodyne offers diatonic scales (major, minor, melodic minor, etc.) and a **Custom** option for exotic or modal material.  
4. **Enter the Chord Progression** – Use the “Chord” field to type the sequence (e.g., “I–V–vi–IV”). Melodyne will display the chord symbols above the grid, and the **Chord Detection** algorithm will align its internal model to those chords.  

> **Tip:** When you set the key and scale, Melodyne automatically updates the **Quantize** snap grid to match the chosen tonalities, but you can still override it per note if artistic intent demands it.

---

## Applying Scale Detection  

### What Scale Detection Does  

When you enable **Scale Detection**, Melodyne scans the entire vocal region and highlights notes that fall outside the selected scale. Out‑of‑scale notes appear in a **different colour** (by default orange) while in‑scale notes stay green. This visual cue is a quick audit of the vocal’s harmonic conformity.

### Enabling and Configuring Scale Detection  

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | In the **Inspector**, locate the **Scale Detection** toggle – it sits just below the Scale dropdown. |
| 2 | Click to turn it **On**. |
